summary.text: Taking \(m=39101\) gives \(N=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1\); a quadratic Lucas–Pocklington argument in \((\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)[\sqrt3]\), using \(N+1=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}\), modular exponentiation of \(2+\sqrt3\), and explicit unit checks for the prime factors \(2,3,100943\), proves that \(N\) is prime. Thus a positive prime-producing step exists, so the least such step cannot be zero.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 n=100943,\qquad m=39101,
\]
and put
\[
 M=2n3^m-1=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1.
\]
We will prove that \(M\) is prime. This gives an explicit positive step, namely \(m=39101\), at which the defining expression for A354747 is prime, and therefore disproves the assertion that \(a(100943)=0\).

The primality proof uses arithmetic in a quadratic ring. All congruences in the finite computation below are modulo \(M\).

## 1. The quadratic ring and the concrete modular computation

For any positive integer \(N\), define
\[
 R_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)[s]/(s^2-3).
\]
Thus an element of \(R_N\) is represented by a pair \((a,b)\), standing for \(a+bs\), and multiplication is
\[
 (a,b)(c,d)=(ac+3bd,\ ad+bc)\pmod N.
\]
The identity is \((1,0)\). Let
\[
 \omega=2+s=(2,1).
\]
Its conjugate is \(\bar\omega=2-s=(2,-1)\), and
\[
 \omega\bar\omega=(2+s)(2-s)=4-s^2=1.
\]
In particular, \(\omega\) is a unit in every \(R_N\).

For the particular modulus \(M\), a finite modular exponentiation gives the following four facts. Set
\[
 y=\omega^{3^{39100}}\in R_M.
\]
Then
\[
 y^{605658}=1,                                                     \tag{1}
\]
and each of
\[
 y^{302829}-1,\qquad y^{201886}-1,\qquad y^6-1                   \tag{2}
\]
is a unit of \(R_M\).

Here is a precise description of the finite computation giving (1) and (2). It is included both to specify the calculation unambiguously and to explain the role of every check. Pairs are reduced coordinatewise modulo \(M\), using
\[
 (a,b)\star(c,d)=((ac+3bd)\bmod M,(ad+bc)\bmod M).
\]
Starting from \((1,0)\), binary repeated squaring with base \((2,1)\) and exponent \(3^{39100}\) produces the pair representing \(y\). Explicitly, if the binary digits of an exponent \(E\), read from most significant to least significant, are \(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_r\), start with \(z_0=(1,0)\) and recursively set
\[
 z_i=z_{i-1}\star z_{i-1}\star (2,1)^{\epsilon_i},
\]
where \((2,1)^0=(1,0)\) and \((2,1)^1=(2,1)\). Then \(z_r=(2,1)^E\) in \(R_M\). The accepted calculation performs exactly this recurrence, grouped into 512-bit blocks, for \(E=3^{39100}\). Applying the same recurrence with base \(y\) gives
\[
 y^{605658}=(1,0).
\]
This is (1).

For each \(e\in\{302829,201886,6\}\), the same pair multiplication computes \(y^e=(A_e,B_e)\). Subtracting \((1,0)\) gives \((A_e-1,B_e)\). The calculation then multiplies this pair by an explicitly computed inverse pair and obtains \((1,0)\) modulo \(M\). Equivalently, one may check the same fact by the norm criterion: the conjugate of \(a+bs\) is \(a-bs\), so
\[
 (a+bs)(a-bs)=a^2-3b^2.
\]
Thus \(a+bs\) is a unit whenever \(a^2-3b^2\) is invertible modulo \(M\). For each of the three computed pairs \((A_e-1,B_e)\), the Euclidean algorithm gives
\[
 \gcd\bigl((A_e-1)^2-3B_e^2,M\bigr)=1.
\]
The extended Euclidean algorithm therefore supplies an inverse for the norm, and multiplying the conjugate by that inverse supplies an inverse for \((A_e-1)+B_es\). These are exactly the three unit assertions in (2).

No probable-prime assumption enters these calculations: they consist solely of integer additions and multiplications, reduction modulo the explicitly defined integer \(M\), binary expansion, and the Euclidean algorithm.

The exponents appearing above come directly from the complete factorization of \(M+1\). Namely,
\[
 M+1=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}
     =3^{39100}\cdot605658,                                      \tag{3}
\]
because
\[
 605658=2\cdot3\cdot100943.
\]
Also,
\[
 \frac{M+1}{2}=3^{39100}\cdot302829,\qquad 302829=3\cdot100943, \tag{4}
\]
\[
 \frac{M+1}{3}=3^{39100}\cdot201886,\qquad 201886=2\cdot100943,\tag{5}
\]
and
\[
 \frac{M+1}{100943}=3^{39100}\cdot6.                            \tag{6}
\]
Consequently, (1) and (3) say
\[
 \omega^{M+1}=1.                                                \tag{7}
\]
Likewise, (2) together with (4)--(6) says that
\[
 \omega^{(M+1)/2}-1,\qquad
 \omega^{(M+1)/3}-1,\qquad
 \omega^{(M+1)/100943}-1                                      \tag{8}
\]
are units in \(R_M\).

The integer \(100943\) is prime. This is a small finite trial-division calculation: its square root is less than \(318\), and division by every prime at most \(317\) leaves a nonzero remainder. Therefore the only prime divisors of
\[
 M+1=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}
\]
are
\[
 2,\quad 3,\quad 100943.                                       \tag{9}
\]
Thus (8) gives the required unit assertion for every prime divisor of \(M+1\).

We now prove why these modular facts force \(M\) to be prime.

## 2. A quadratic-ring primality criterion

We use the following criterion.

**Criterion.** Let \(N\ge2\), with neither \(2\) nor \(3\) dividing \(N\). In
\[
 R_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)[s]/(s^2-3)
\]
let \(\omega=2+s\). Suppose
\[
 \omega^{N+1}=1,                                                \tag{10}
\]
and suppose that for every prime \(q\mid N+1\), the element
\[
 \omega^{(N+1)/q}-1                                             \tag{11}
\]
is a unit of \(R_N\). Then \(N\) is prime.

**Proof of the criterion.** Suppose, to the contrary, that \(N\) is composite. Let \(p\) be its least prime divisor. Since \(N\) is composite,
\[
 p^2\le N.                                                      \tag{12}
\]
Because neither \(2\) nor \(3\) divides \(N\), we have \(p\ne2,3\). Thus \(p\) is odd and \(3\not\equiv0\pmod p\).

Reduction modulo \(p\) defines a ring homomorphism
\[
 R_N\longrightarrow R_p,
 \qquad
 R_p=(\mathbb F_p)[s]/(s^2-3).
\]
Write \(\omega_p\) for the image of \(\omega\). Equation (10) gives
\[
 \omega_p^{N+1}=1.                                              \tag{13}
\]
Moreover, a unit maps to a unit. Hence (11) implies
\[
 \omega_p^{(N+1)/q}\ne1                                       \tag{14}
\]
for every prime \(q\mid N+1\): if equality held, the image of the unit in (11) would be zero, but zero is not a unit in the nonzero ring \(R_p\).

Let \(d\) be the multiplicative order of \(\omega_p\). This order exists because \(\omega_p\) is a unit; indeed \((2+s)(2-s)=1\). From (13),
\[
 d\mid N+1.                                                     \tag{15}
\]
In fact
\[
 d=N+1.                                                         \tag{16}
\]
To see this, suppose that \(d<N+1\). Then \((N+1)/d>1\), so it has a prime divisor \(q\). We may write \(N+1=dqk\). Therefore \(d\mid(N+1)/q\), which would give
\[
 \omega_p^{(N+1)/q}=1,
\]
contrary to (14). This proves (16).

We next obtain a second, much smaller, possible multiple of the order of \(\omega_p\). In characteristic \(p\), the binomial theorem gives
\[
 (2+s)^p=2^p+s^p=2+s^p.
\]
Since \(s^2=3\) and \(p\) is odd,
\[
 s^p=s(s^2)^{(p-1)/2}=s\,3^{(p-1)/2}.
\]
By Fermat's theorem,
\[
 \left(3^{(p-1)/2}\right)^2=3^{p-1}=1\pmod p.
\]
Over the field \(\mathbb F_p\), an element whose square is \(1\) is either \(1\) or \(-1\). Hence
\[
 3^{(p-1)/2}=1\quad\hbox{or}\quad 3^{(p-1)/2}=-1\pmod p.
\]
There are therefore two cases.

* If \(3^{(p-1)/2}=1\), then
  \[
  \omega_p^p=2+s=\omega_p.
  \]
  Since \(\omega_p\) is a unit, cancellation gives
  \[
  \omega_p^{p-1}=1.
  \]
  Thus its order divides \(p-1\).

* If \(3^{(p-1)/2}=-1\), then
  \[
  \omega_p^p=2-s=\bar\omega_p.
  \]
  Multiplying by \(\omega_p\), and using
  \((2+s)(2-s)=1\), gives
  \[
  \omega_p^{p+1}=1.
  \]
  Thus its order divides \(p+1\).

Combining either conclusion with (16), we obtain
\[
 N+1\mid p-1\quad\hbox{or}\quad N+1\mid p+1.                  \tag{17}
\]
If \(N+1\mid p-1\), then \(N+1\le p-1\), which is impossible since \(p\le N\). If \(N+1\mid p+1\), then \(N+1\le p+1\), so \(N\le p\). Since \(p\mid N\), this forces \(N=p\), contradicting the assumption that \(N\) is composite. Equivalently, one can combine \(N\le p\) with (12): for \(p\ge2\), the inequalities \(p^2\le N\le p\) are impossible. Both cases in (17) are contradictions. Therefore \(N\) is prime. This proves the criterion.

## 3. Applying the criterion to \(M\)

The integer
\[
 M=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1
\]
is at least \(2\). It is odd, so \(2\nmid M\), and it is congruent to \(-1\pmod3\), so \(3\nmid M\).

Equation (7), obtained by modular exponentiation, states
\[
 \omega^{M+1}=1\quad\text{in }R_M.
\]
By (9), every prime divisor \(q\) of \(M+1\) is one of \(2,3,100943\). For these three possibilities, the three unit calculations in (8) state precisely that
\[
 \omega^{(M+1)/q}-1
\]
is a unit in \(R_M\). All hypotheses of the quadratic-ring criterion are therefore satisfied. It follows that
\[
 M=2\cdot100943\cdot3^{39101}-1
\]
is prime.

## 4. Disproof of the conjectured sequence value

For \(n=100943\), let
\[
 S=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\ge1\text{ and }2\cdot100943\cdot3^r-1
\text{ is prime}\}.
\]
The result just proved says that
\[
 39101\in S.
\]
Thus \(S\) is nonempty. By the definition of A354747, \(a(100943)\) is the least element of \(S\). Every element of \(S\) is at least \(1\), so its least element is also at least \(1\). In particular,
\[
 a(100943)\ne0.
\]
Indeed, the argument gives the explicit upper bound \(a(100943)\le39101\), although it does not need to assert that \(39101\) is the least successful exponent.

Hence the conjecture \(a(100943)=0\) is false.
